record.original_question: Is every (2k − 1)-connected graph guaranteed to have a spanning bipartite subgraph that is k-connected?

evidence.quote: Is it true that every (2k − 1)-connected graph has a k-connected spanning bipartite subgraph?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let $k\ge 1$ be an integer. A graph $G=(V,E)$ is called $m$-connected if $|V|>m$ and for every set $S\subseteq V$ with $|S|<m$ the graph $G-S$ is connected. A spanning subgraph of $G$ is a subgraph with vertex set equal to $V$. A graph is bipartite if its vertex set admits a partition into two parts such that every edge has one endpoint in each part.

Determine whether the following statement is true: every $(2k-1)$-connected graph $G$ contains a spanning bipartite subgraph that is $k$-connected.
artifact.status_search_result: This is a question in the spirit of Thomassen's 1989 conjecture on spanning bipartite k-connected subgraphs. Partial results give f(k,n)-type bounds: Delcourt–Ferber showed f(k,n) ≤ 10^{10} k^3 log n, and a more recent result improves this to O(k^2 log n). The conjecture (and in particular the sharp form with f(k)=2k-1) remains open.

status_evidence.title: On a Conjecture of Thomassen
status_evidence.snippet: In 1989, Thomassen asked whether there is an integer-valued function f(k) such that every f(k)-connected graph admits a spanning, bipartite k-connected subgraph.
status_evidence.claim: The conjecture is attributed to Thomassen (1989) and is still being studied.

status_evidence.title: Highly connected graphs have highly connected spanning bipartite subgraphs
status_evidence.snippet: Recent improvement showing f(k,n) ≤ O(k^2 log n).
status_evidence.claim: Recent progress yields polylogarithmic bounds; the conjecture remains open.
